NextItNet uses causal dilated convolutions and residual connections to capture ordered history, with autoregressive supervision across sequence positions. Thus, random-prefix truncation can change both available context and supervised examples; an accuracy gain alone does not establish stronger context dependence. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163). For stride-one convolutions, theoretical receptive-field width is R = 1 + Σℓ(kℓ−1)dℓ, counting every temporal convolution separately. Actual influence can occupy substantially less than this structural bound: general CNN research distinguishes effective from theoretical receptive fields, although it does not establish NextItNet-specific behavior. [Effective receptive-field study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.04128).

The located sources do not provide the requested fully controlled NextItNet suffix-response experiment. A practical diagnostic proposal: evaluate each frozen model on identical users, targets and fixed negative candidates across nested suffix lengths; report paired HR@10 changes, target-margin changes and category macro averages. Keep tensor width and retained-item positions fixed through left padding, and read the final nonpadding position. For training comparisons, preserve identical supervised target positions, negatives, loss normalization and update counts while varying only each target’s accessible prefix. Separately shift identical suffixes with controlled position IDs, where applicable, to isolate positional effects. Audit padding and normalization: with strictly local operations, changing items outside R cannot affect the final score; changes suggest additional information paths or an implementation issue. Training-prefix curves remain in-sample diagnostics; validation curves assess generalization. These controls are proposed methodology, not published evidence that truncation improves NextItNet.
